newsitem.title: USA: Advanta card losses seen part of trend.
newsitem.headline: Advanta card losses seen part of trend.

text.p: Although credit-card issuer Advanta Corp shocked the industry Monday with the news that it will record a loss in the first quarter of 1997, analysts said the company is caught up an industry trend that varies in its impact considerably from company to company.

"Advanta apparently didn't price their products well," said Robert McKinley, president of RAM Resarch Group, a Frederick, Md-based research firm. He noted that Advanta was a big issuer of cards with no annual fee and low introductory rates.

In a telephone interview, Alex "Pete" Hart, chief executive of Advanta, said setting the appropriate pricing is a key to restoring profitability. The company said it expects to have a profit in the second quarter and a profit of $1.50 per share for the year 1997, notwithstanding a loss of about $0.44 per share for the first quarter.

"There is no question that charge-offs have been rising at most of the banks I talk to but they are unwilling to predict where that may peak out," said Raphael Soifer, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman.
"Different banks have different portfolios and because one company is having problems does not mean there would be problems of a comparable magnitude at another company," said Soifer.

MBNA Corp, which like Advanta is a "monoline" issuer specializing in cards, said Monday that its loan losses this year through February were 3.70 percent compared to 3.45 percent for 1996 excluding the sale of certain charged-off accounts in 1966. MBNA said it attributed its performance to the way it controls accounts and its management practices.
Advanta said it expects its loss rate on credit cards to be in the 6.5-7.5 percent range this year, compared to 3.2 percent in the first quarter of 1996.

Alison Emmerich, an analyst at Standard & Poor's Corp, said there have been some instances of loss rates getting to the 7.0 percent area or higher. But she said the loss rate cannot be viewed in isolation. "The issue here is how much higher charegeoffs are being offset by higher yields," she said.
Some lenders, she said, target sub-prime borrowers and expect to offset higher losses with a more expensive product.
Emmerich said a concern is that the loss rates have been creeping up while the U.S. economy remains on a growth footing. "We're supposed to be in a good economic environment," she said.
She said that while even higher loss rates could well be manageable "for a lot of companies they could be unmanageable if we're in a recession."
"We are already seeing tightening across the industry," RAM Research's McKinley said, with spending limits coming down and card holders being hit with higher interest rates.
Emmerich noted that as any one company moves to tighten, it has to worry about losing customers to other issuers.
Advanta noted in its press release that a rise in consumer bankruptcies contributed to its problems.

McKinley said a problem with the bankruptcies is that they have come "out of the blue" unlike earlier times when a card holder would become delinquent in his or her payments and then filed for bankruptcy.
Two other monoline companies, First USA Inc and Capital One Financial Corp were not immediately available for comment on their loss ratios.
First USA reached an agreement in January to be acquired by Banc One Corp.
